| `trust-tasks-didcomm-v1` | crates.io | `0.24.6` → `0.24.7` | patch |
| `trust-tasks-https` | crates.io | `0.24.6` → `0.24.7` | patch |
| `trust-tasks-proof` | crates.io | `0.24.6` → `0.24.7` | patch |
| `trust-tasks-rs` | crates.io | `0.24.6` → `0.24.7` | patch |
| `trust-tasks-tsp` | crates.io | `0.24.6` → `0.24.7` | patch |
| `@openvtc/trust-tasks` | npm | `0.21.13` → `0.21.14` | patch |
| `github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/trust-tasks-go` | Go (tag `trust-tasks-go/v0.3.14`) | `0.3.13` → `0.3.14` | patch |
| `trust_tasks` | pub.dev | `0.3.13` → `0.3.14` | patch |

What merging does, per registry (all in `publish.yml`, each keyed on "this
version is not published yet"):

- **crates.io** — `release-plz-release` tags `<crate>-v<version>`, publishes in
  dependency order and creates a GitHub Release per crate. Bump levels come from
  `cargo-semver-checks`.
- **npm** — `publish-npm` publishes with OIDC provenance and tags
  `<prefix>-v<version>`.
- **Go** — `publish-go` builds, vets and tests, then pushes the tag, which *is*
  the publication. **Irreversible**: proxy.golang.org never forgets a tag.
- **pub.dev** — `tag-dart` verifies against the *published* core and pushes the
  tag; `publish-dart.yml` publishes from it.

The npm, Go and Dart bumps are only as accurate as the commit subjects — nothing
checks their APIs the way `cargo-semver-checks` checks the crates. Look for a
missing `!` before merging.

This branch is regenerated from `main` on every push, so do not commit to it —
edits are force-pushed away. See RELEASING.md.

title: feat(git-ns): administrator reads as Trust Tasks (#686)
body:
feat(git-ns): administrator reads as Trust Tasks (#686)

* feat(git-ns): administrator reads as Trust Tasks

Six VTC git-ns console REST reads had no Trust Task equivalent: the admin
console's Repos plugin (rights, jobs, projection, accounts) and activity
feed were served only over a bearer admin session, with no signed,
transport-agnostic path.

New specs:

- git-ns/right/list/0.1 — the whole-community rights picture (recorded and
  v0.1 role-derived grants), each row's subjectMember/granterDeparted.
  A new spec rather than a git-ns/view revision: the role-derived rows are
  not RightRecords (no granter, no grant time) and the administrative
  membership facts are not member-facing, so folding them into view/0.5's
  shared RightRecord would widen every other consumer of that component.
- git-ns/right/issued-by-departed/0.1 — recorded rights grouped by a
  departed granter, alongside the community's cascade_on_departure policy.
- git-ns/bridge/job/list/0.1 — the bridge job queue, scoped to administered
  namespaces like git-ns/namespace/list and git-ns/repo/list.
- git-ns/projection/show/0.1 — what is published to the Trust Registry,
  and how many records the next reconciliation pass will change.
- git-ns/account/list/0.1 — every member's linked forge account,
  community-wide, since git-ns/view only returns the caller's own.
- git-ns/activity/list/0.1 — rights changes, drift and bridge jobs
  interleaved into one timeline, scoped like the namespace/repo listings.

All six declare proof REQUIRED, an Authorization section naming either the
community-administrator capability (rights, issued-by-departed,
projection, accounts — matching the REST handlers' SuperAdminAuth gate) or
namespace-administrator standing (jobs, activity — matching the namespace
and repo listings' pattern), and a cursor/limit paged list shape.
git-ns/_shared/0.5 adds AdminRightRow and RightOrigin, the row shape right/list
and right/issued-by-departed share.

Regenerated all four bindings (Rust, TypeScript, Go, Dart).

title: feat(auth): proxied authenticate and session-key refresh
body:
## Summary

webvh#238 kept three REST auth routes because no Trust Task covered them: the VTA-proxied SIOPv2 login (`POST /api/auth/challenge` + `POST /api/auth/`) and the session-key-bound refresh (`POST /api/auth/refresh`). This PR closes both gaps so webvh can delete its last REST auth routes.

- **`auth/authenticate/0.3`** — adds an optional proxied form. `payload.principal` names the VID being authenticated as when it differs from the document's `issuer`; `payload.delegationEvidence` carries whatever the auth service's own policy requires as evidence that `issuer` (the delegate, e.g. a holder's VTA) may act for `principal`. The resulting `Session.subject` is `principal`; the new `Session.actor` (shared `_shared/0.3` Session schema) records the delegate, so audit and revocation never conflate the two. The ordinary (self-authenticating) form from 0.2 is unchanged, including the `sessionKey` binding.
- **`auth/refresh/0.2`** — accepts a `proof` made by the session key bound at login (`auth/authenticate/0.2`/`0.3`), required in addition to the refresh token whenever the located session carries one (`sessionKeyProofRequired` otherwise). Adds an absolute session lifetime rule: refresh MUST NOT advance `Session.expiresAt` past `Session.absoluteExpiresAt`, refusing with `sessionLifetimeExceeded` once reached — the session key is never accepted as approval/step-up authority, only as a binding check layered on the bearer token.

Both specs add an `## Authorization` section (framework 0.6.0, required for consequential tasks), the four Security & Privacy sub-headings covering delegation abuse, stolen session keys and refresh-token theft with valid/invalid examples, and `## Changes from` sections.

All four bindings (Rust, TypeScript, Go, Dart) regenerated and cross-checked.

## Test plan

- [x] `npm run validate`
- [x] `npm run check-bindings`
- [x] `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs -- specs::auth` (81 passed)
- [x] `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features validate -- specs::auth::authenticate::v0_3 specs::auth::refresh::v0_2` (8 passed, including `rejects_invalid_examples`)

title: feat(vtc-service)!: the community's REST-only admin surfaces are signed Trust Tasks
body:
## Summary

VTC batch 3, part 2 (stacked on #1834). The community's REST-only admin surfaces from trust-tasks #680 move onto the Trust Task spine (`trust_tasks::surface_tasks`). Authority is the signer's ACL row, read at execution, and matches each bearer route:

| task | authority |
|---|---|
| `vtc/community/{branding,requested-attributes,join-discovery}/show/0.1` | any entry (the route took any session) |
| `vtc/community/{branding,requested-attributes,join-discovery}/update/0.1` | `Admin` |
| `vtc/schemas/{register,list,show,delete}/0.1`, `vtc/schemas/accepts/{register,list,show,delete}/0.1` | `Admin` |
| `vtc/vetting/vetters/grants/list/0.1`, `vtc/vetting/auto-grant/{show,update}/0.1`, `vtc/vetting/revocations/list/0.1` | `Admin` |
| `vtc/relationships/{suspend,restore}/0.1` | the edge's issuer or an `Admin`; anyone else gets `notFound` |
| `vtc/join-requests/vetting/show/0.1`, `vtc/join-requests/query/0.1` | `Admin` |
| `vtc/rooms/list/0.1` | `Admin` (host admin view, outside `rooms/*` per I5) |

Notes:
- **Suspend/restore**: the issuer is the document's signer, so the issuer's own proof replaces the route's `pop` authorization. A pairwise-DID edge is suspended by a document that DID signs.
- **Schemas**: `delete` now refuses with `inUse` (a SHOULD the old route skipped) when an Accepts criterion's DCQL names the type, with `details.criterionIds`. `accepts/register` refuses in the spec's order: `invalidQuery`, `unregisteredType`, `unregisteredStatementType`, `invalidVetting`, `notPublishable`.
- **Listings** page in memory with an offset cursor (`o<n>`). A cursor from anywhere else is refused.
- **Error codes**: every declared code is witnessed in `tests/surface_verbs_spine.rs`, except `accepts/register:notPublishable`. That one is baselined (UNWITNESSED 8→9) because no schema-valid payload reaches it; the reason is in the census.
- **Console**: every call on these surfaces is a signed document: vetting (grants, auto-grant, withdrawals, join vetting facts, criteria), branding, join discovery, rooms. Response shapes the removed routes described are kept in the openapi components, so the console's wire types are still generated.

## Routes

Removed: `GET`/`PUT /v1/community/join-discovery`, `POST`/`GET /v1/schemas`, `GET`/`DELETE /v1/schemas/{type_uri}`, `POST`/`GET /v1/schemas/accepts`, `GET`/`DELETE /v1/schemas/accepts/{id}`, `POST /v1/relationships/{id}/suspend`, `POST /v1/relationships/{id}/restore`, `GET /v1/join-requests/{id}/vetting`, `POST /v1/join-requests/query`, `GET /v1/rooms`.

Kept because `vtc-client` still calls them: `GET`/`PUT /v1/community/branding`, `GET`/`PUT /v1/community/requested-attributes`, `GET /v1/vetting/vetters`, `GET`/`PUT /v1/vetting/auto-grant`, `GET /v1/vetting/revocations`.

* feat(vtc-service)!: the policy log and the community's DID log are signed Trust Tasks

policy/{list,get,active,upsert,activate}, vtc/policies/test and
did-management/did/register are served by the spine
(trust_tasks::policy_tasks) on every transport, with the signer's ACL row
as authority: Admin for the policy verbs, an unrestricted Admin for the
DID log, as the bearer routes' AdminAuth and SuperAdminAuth asked.
policy/activate refuses a purpose the revision does not decide. The

Per-type document limits come from the specifications: size.rs reads the
codegen'd maxDocumentBytes (schema_index::max_document_bytes_for) and keeps
an interim entry only for policy/upsert and did/register, whose specs
declare none yet. A raised limit applies to a served type only, and only
when the claimed issuer holds a live ACL entry (or is a signing key
delegated by one), looked up before verification. The HTTPS cap is the
largest served limit; a refusal does not echo an oversized type.

tasks surface_tasks serves, built from the types the handlers emit, and
the OpenAPI route-group test no longer expects /v1/rooms or /v1/schemas,
which the spine replaced; both join the signed-only list with the other
routes this PR removed.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: chore(vetting-pcs): use the published predicate-credential-system crate (#396)
body:
chore(vetting-pcs): use the published predicate-credential-system crate (#396)

* feat(vetting): hidden-vetter admission (ZKP) on the Predicate Credential System

Bob proves to a VTC that k distinct, currently eligible vetters vetted
him, without the VTC learning which. Development branch: nothing here is
wired into the client flow yet, and nothing is published.

- openvtc-vetting-pcs (publish = false): the corrected design of
  docs/design/vetting-hidden-vetters-pcs.md end to end. The VTC side as a
  local stand-in (epoch labels on the vetter class, member-to-id binding,
  token drip with per-label spent sets, event mode, withdrawal by tag),
  and the vetter and applicant engines that belong in the VTA.
- Counting is vta-sdk's own vetting::requirements::evaluate, unchanged,
  with the vetter's tag where the vetter's DID used to be: the join
  policy needs no change.
- Application contexts are JCS (RFC 8785) bytes, so both sides build the
  same bytes.
- 14 end-to-end tests, including the adversarial cases: double-spent
  token, tokens and metadata moved between attestations, forged
  withdrawal, a twin key pair for one member, replayed opening proofs.

vendor/: predicate-credential-system at aa57efd plus one patch, which
adds application contexts to the construction. Vendored because the
crate is not on crates.io and the branch carrying the patch is not
pushed; the patch is kept as a patch so it can be offered upstream.

cargo-deny passes unchanged: a vendored path dependency is not a git
source, so [sources] needed no allow-git entry. The path dependency
carries a version so it is not a wildcard. deny.toml records both.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* refactor(vetting-pcs): split the verifier from the issuer, and pin the wire format

The VTC service needs to check a submission from public parameters
alone, and so does a client that wants to know what the VTC will make of
what it holds. Verifier now holds the helper key, the token verifier,
the spent set and the counting; Vtc keeps the secrets on top of it.

- verifier.rs: Submission, StatementRecord, Decision, submit, evaluate,
  withdraw. TokenVerifier splits out of TokenIssuer the same way, so one
  spent set serves minting and verification.
- wire.rs: extensions.hiddenVetting, the JSON both repos must agree on.
  Binary values are multibase over the validated canonical encoding.
- The submission now carries the id-to-persona binding, and the verifier
  recomputes and compares it instead of trusting it. A tampered join DID
  is refused there rather than at the proof.
- tests/fixtures/submission.json: generated, and read back by the VTI
  branch's own verifier. 5.4 KB, against the VTC's 16 KiB extensions cap.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(vetting-pcs): pluggable spent-token ledger

The VTC has to remember spent serials across requests and its store is
async, while verification is not. TokenVerifier now takes a SpentLedger:
the in-memory one is the default, and the VTC swaps in its own, which
preloads the rows a submission touches and commits what was taken.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(vetting): read a community's hidden-vetting parameters, and honour criticality

A community that counts statements from a zero-knowledge proof publishes
the parameters under vetting.ext, in a namespace it controls, and marks
that namespace in vetting.extCritical (dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#23,
dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#600, both merged).

- vetting::hidden reads the mode from a criterion. A namespace marked
  critical that this build does not implement stops the application with
  a notice the applicant sees, rather than ignoring it: a client that
  ignored it would gather named statements and present them to a
  criterion whose purpose is that it never receives them, and neither
  side would learn a downgrade had happened. An UNMARKED namespace stays
  ignorable, which is the framework's default and why marking has to be
  deliberate.
- Application carries the parameters, defaulted absent, so a config that
  has never seen one round-trips unchanged.
- adopt_manifest and fetch_manifest take and return the payload AS
  RECEIVED. This is not a convenience: a generated criterion carries the
  members its schema names and drops the rest, so re-serialising the
  parse produces a criterion missing ext and a requirementsDigest that
  no longer matches what was sent. Both manifest paths — the DIDComm
  reply and the public probe — now read the raw bytes.

openvtc-core keeps its own HiddenParams type meanwhile: vetting.ext is a
declared member as of manifest 0.2, so it survives the parse once this
workspace takes a trust-tasks-rs release carrying it, and reading it
from the raw criterion works either way.

1482 workspace tests pass; clippy and cargo-deny are clean.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(vetting): the ZKP onboarding flow, end to end on the client

An applicant can now be admitted under a hidden-vetting criterion
without the community learning who vetted them, driven through the
client's own types.

- openvtc-vetting-pcs gains CommunityParams: the PUBLISHED half of a
  deployment, which is all a member ever holds. The applicant and vetter
  engines work from it rather than from the community object, so the
  tests drive the code path a client does.
- snapshot: storable forms of both engines, so an application survives a
  restart. A restored vetter attests with the same key, which is what
  keeps one vetter counting once (§13 C2). They carry usk and say so.
- vetting::hidden gains the flow: start, attest, receive, prove.
- Application mints its own key when it adopts a hidden criterion,
  verifies each attestation at the session rather than at submit, and
  carries the proof in join_extensions beside the requirements digest.
  join_flow builds it before the presentation.
- tests/hidden_vetting_onboarding.rs runs both halves: the flow through
  the hidden API, and the same flow through Application — manifest,
  two sessions, proof, extensions, admission. It asserts the facts the
  policy sees carry tags rather than vetters, and that the submission
  fits the VTC's 16 KiB extensions cap.

Known gap: the proof is bound to a challenge this client mints, not one
the VTC issued, and the service does not yet check that it issued it.
Replay is held off by the spent-token set and the one-open-request rule
meanwhile; a VTC-issued nonce is the fix and needs a manifest or submit
round trip to carry it.

1485 workspace tests pass; clippy and cargo-deny clean.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* refactor(vetting-pcs): keep the mirrored files self-contained

HeldToken and the multibase encode helpers moved to the modules the VTC
half already mirrors — token and scheme — so the VTI copy needs nothing
from the member-side snapshot module that only openvtc has.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs(vetting): say how to run the ZKP onboarding flow, and what a real run still needs

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs(vetting): a reference run — ten vetters, three vet, one admission

An example that prints every artifact the flow produces, with its byte
size, so the reference set is output rather than description: the two
key pairs, a vetter's root credential and token, the published criterion
with its critical namespace, the applicant's identifier, three
attestations with the statement facts that travel beside them, the
submission, and the facts the community counts.

The committed output is what the seeded run produces, so a change that
alters the wire shows up as a diff here.

Sizes from the run: helper and token key 336 B each, root credential
96 B, token serial 32 B with a 96 B signature, attestation 248 B, proof
952 B at k=3, whole submission 3,962 B against the VTC's 16,384 B cap.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs(vetting): run the reference flow through the real ceremony

The first version of this example invented the parts it did not exercise:
DIDs that were strings, an identity commitment and a card digest that
were decorative. Those are exactly the values an attestation binds, so
inventing them left the interesting half untested.

It now runs the real thing. Ten did:key identities with real Ed25519
keys; ten community-signed role credentials; and for each of the three
vetting sessions a ticket, a session with a match code, a Vetting Card
the applicant signs and the vetter verifies against the resolver, and a
statement draft — whose identityCommitment and cardDigestMultibase are
what the attestation carries. Then the proof, the submission, and the
community's decision.

It also asserts the two things the design claims: no tag equals any
enrolled PCS identifier, and no vetter DID appears anywhere in the
submission. And presentable_statements() returns none, because on this
path no statement naming a vetter is ever made.

Committed output refreshed.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* reference run: mint the admission credentials and emit every VC in full

The run stopped at the community's decision, so the artefact that a real
admission ends with — the membership credential — was missing, and with it
the question of whether the hidden path issues everything a named one does.

Admission now mints what vtc-service's Admit effect mints: the VMC against a
revocation slot (id and credentialStatus spliced onto the body and covered by
one proof, as LocalSigner::sign_doc does), the role VEC at the granted role,
and the member's own reciprocal VMC through openvtc-core's build_member_vmc —
which digests the grant as it arrived, so the two halves bind. Each proof is
verified in the run, and no vetter DID appears in any of them.

Every credential is now emitted in full rather than one per kind, so the
output is usable as a test-vector set: each VC is self-contained and verifies
against the did:key in its issuer. step00 records the seeds every identity is
derived from, and states plainly which values are stable across runs and which
are not. step11 is the inventory: what is issued here, what is deliberately
not (a signed vetting statement would name its vetter; a VRC names both ends),
and what a live deployment adds.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* design: record what a hidden admission issues, and what it deliberately does not

The credential question is answered structurally: the hidden path rejoins the
named one at vetting_facts, so Admit and issue_member_credentials are reached
unchanged and a live hidden admission already mints the VMC pair and role VEC.
The table records the five credentials that are not issued and why — including
the one that matters for the design: a community that required a VRC pair with
its vetters could not run hidden vetting, because a VRC names both ends.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* hidden vetting: the minting half, a published drip rate, and the exchanges as wire

The community's side of enrolment and the drip was one type holding keys and
three HashSets holding the rules. The keys move to `issuer::Issuer`, which
signs and counts nothing, so the rules can live where they belong — in a
store, on the VTI side, where they survive a restart. `Vtc` keeps its sets and
delegates the signing, so what a test drives here is what the service runs
there.

The quota was the hole this opened up: `TokenIssuer::issue` checked the label,
the tick and every opening proof, and never how many requests were in the
batch, so a vetter could ask for a thousand tokens in one tick and be served
them. `Issuer::issue_tokens` takes the rate and refuses before anything is
signed; the rate is published as `dripPerTick` so a vetter knows what to ask
for, and an event label carries its own, higher one, which is the reason event
labels exist.

Issuance randomness is an argument rather than an `OsRng` reached for inside,
because a signing routine that samples its own randomness cannot be pinned by
a test — and the cross-repo wire fixture is exactly a pinned test.

The vetter's half of both exchanges splits into request and accept
(`enrolment_request`/`accept_enrolment`, `drip_request`/`accept_drip`) over
wire types that name what travels, so adding the Trust Tasks is plumbing. The
reference run drives those halves and shows both refusals, and the community's
challenge: the same submission replayed, and one bound to a challenge nobody
issued, are both refused in the run.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* design: date §17 correctly and name the service-path test

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* vetter: attest through the desk, on the hidden path

A vetter could not attest without a screen, and the screen could not attest
without a path that did not sign anything. This is that path.

VettingBook::attest_hidden reuses statement_draft to build what it will not
sign, which is the point: one checklist, one set of refusals, one place that
decides a claim is not on the card or a documentary method relied on nothing.
Only the last step differs - the engine spends a token and produces an
attestation carrying a tag where an issuer would be, and the desk closes the
request into Attested exactly as the named path closes it. Nothing is added to
the issued list: there is no statement to withdraw, and hidden withdrawal is
the token spend-set and label rotation instead.

The applicant's PCS identifier reaches the vetter in the request's ext member,
the framework's own extension point, so a community that does not run hidden
vetting still sees a vetting/request it understands. The engine and the
community's published parameters live together on the book, because by the
time a criterion has been parsed into VettingRequirements the parameters are
gone - they live in ext, which the parse drops.

Delivery is vetting/attestation/0.1, now a published task. The inbound arm
verifies on arrival rather than at submit, and deliberately does not record
the delivering sender beside the attestation: keeping it would rebuild, in the
applicant's own store, the link the exchange removes.

The reference example drives the desk path now, so the run that produces the
vector set is the run the screen makes: three sessions, three attestations,
admitted, replay refused.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* applicant: say that this community hides its vetters

The one line the applicant reads about what is being asked of them said
nothing about the only thing that makes this criterion different. A criterion
that hides its vetters looked exactly like one that does not.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* client: enrolment, the drip and the challenge over the wire

The vetter could attest and the applicant could prove, but neither could get
what it needed from the community without a person doing it by hand. Three
exchanges close that, against the specifications published on the
hidden-vetting-tasks branch.

Enrolment and the drip are split into request and accept on both sides, so the
blinding state and the wallet's pending serials live where they belong. The
enrolment blinding is held in memory for one round trip and deliberately not
persisted: it is useless without the answer and dangerous to keep past it, so
an answer that arrives after a restart is dropped and the client asks again -
which costs nothing, because a request never unblinded issued no credential
anyone will count.

The schedule is the part worth reading twice. `due` decides what a vetter owes
a community from the clock and the labels, and it is never given a wallet: a
client that drew when it was running low would publish, in the timing of its
own requests, how much vetting it had been doing. A vetter that has been
offline asks for the current tick and not the ones it missed - the same answer
a vetter who was present and idle gets, and that symmetry is the point.

The applicant now binds the community's challenge rather than one it minted
itself, and says so while it waits for one. Its checklist counts held
attestations instead of reporting zero while it holds three; the count is the
applicant's own estimate, because two attestations from one vetter carry the
same tag and the tag is inside the proof, out of reach here. The community's
count at submit is the authority.

The payload types are written rather than generated, for the reason recorded
in the design doc: the bindings are trust-tasks-rs 0.22 and this graph pins
^0.21. The service side validates its half against the published schemas; when
the release lands both halves delete their types and import the generated
ones.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs(vetting): close §19.3 and add a standalone hidden-vetting example

The wire is finished on both halves, so §19.3 stops being a list of what is
missing and says what runs: the three tasks dispatched and driven by an
integration test, the client's request/accept split, the clock-driven schedule
that is never shown a balance, and the four screens.

The example is the protocol with nothing around it — ten vetters, three
attestations, one proof, and then what the community can and cannot tell. It
exists because the privacy argument is only convincing if it can be read in one
sitting, and reading it across the engine, the desk, the tasks and the UI is not
that.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(vetting): event mode over the wire

A vetter's ordinary rate is a few tokens a tick whether or not they have vetted
anyone. That is right for ordinary weeks and wrong for a conference desk, and
§5.1's answer is deliberately not a bigger drip: a separate token label for a
named event, with its own rate, its own expiry, and a group large enough that a
spend under it still hides one. `vtc/vetting/vetters/event-mode/0.1` is the
vetter's half of that, and it is only ever a request — approving an event is an
act by somebody else, because a task the vetter could send is a task a vetter
could be made to send.

The schedule now keys its tick per label, because a vetter at a conference owes
two draws a day. Dropping the monthly one for the three days of a summit would
say, in the timing of the requests alone, that those three days were a summit.
It draws only under events the community has approved us for: a published label
says an event exists, never that we are in its group.

`e` on the desk offers the community's published menu — each event and tier,
with the event's own days as the window — and says the price before it is asked
for: an attestation made there says "someone vetting at this event" rather than
"someone in this community". The window is the event's rather than the
vetter's, because naming your own days says which days of a conference you
expect to be at the desk. What comes back carries a group count and never a
roster, which is the most a member can be told about a set they are hiding in.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs(vetting): name the approval surface and the narrowing of §5.1

The design said an admin or moderator approves an event via `vetter_rate.rego`.
The policy hook is not built; the admin route that already carries these
parameters is. Worth saying which, and worth saying that the rule §5.1 was
protecting did not go with it — a self-approval opens nothing because the check
lives where the tokens are served, not where the configuration is written.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs(vetting): the generated types are not waiting for a release

This branch has said all along that the hand-written payload types wait on a
`trust-tasks-rs` release. They do not: 0.22 is published, #618 merged the four
specifications, and #619 publishes 0.22.2 carrying them.

What they wait on is the 0.22 line reaching the VTI graph, which resolves
0.21.17 because affinidi-messaging-sdk, the mediator and the four
trust-tasks companions are all on 0.21 and re-export trust-tasks-rs types.
Bumping one workspace gives two nodes that cannot unify. That is a five-crate
queue and none of it is ours, which is a different thing to plan around than a
release we could ask for.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs(vetting): event mode is merged upstream

trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf #620. All five specifications the hidden path
needs are now on main; nothing on the specification side is outstanding.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(vetting): a vetter's client can reach hidden vetting at all

Two of the three things standing between "the wire is closed" and "two
processes can do this" are on this side, and both were absent rather than
broken.

A vetter's engine was never created. `HiddenVetterState` existed in a test and
in the reference example and nowhere else, so a running client had no vetter
half: no enrolment, no tokens, nothing to attest with. `hidden::vetter_start`
mints the key pair from the community's published parameters, and the desk makes
one the first time it finds a community that both publishes the mode and has
named us a vetter. Both halves of that matter — published parameters say the
mode exists, never that we are in it.

`member` in that snapshot is the persona's DID and not a label. It is bound
into every opening proof the drip sends and checked by the community against the
signer, so a snapshot built under any other name draws tokens that are refused
and the refusal says nothing about why. The doc comment says so where someone
would otherwise pass a display name.

And nothing ever fetched the manifest of a community we only vet for. An
applicant refreshes because it is applying; a vetter has no application, and the
manifest is the only place a community says it hides its vetters. `m` on the
desk now asks each of them.

The fixture test is what stands in for an integration test across two
repositories that cannot compile each other: the community's emitted shape,
pinned, read by the code that will read it live — plus its negative, that the
*stored* shape is not mistaken for the published one.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vetting): hidden vetting's community-bound tasks ride the DIDComm envelope

The merge of #372 made the VTC-bound carriage an allow-list, and the four
hidden-vetting tasks (pcs-root, pcs-tokens, event-mode, pcs-challenge) were not
on it, so they would have gone task-typed and been refused by a VTC with #1687.
The attestation stays task-typed: it is a peer leg.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* chore(vetting-pcs): use the published predicate-credential-system crate

The application-context patch merged upstream at
https://github.com/OpenVTC/predicate-credential-system, which is now published
to crates.io as v0.1.0 (see that repo's RELEASING.md for the release-plz /
Trusted Publishing setup). openvtc-vetting-pcs depends on it by version instead
of a vendored path now; vendor/predicate-credential-system,
vendor/0001-pcs-application-contexts.patch and vendor/PROVENANCE.md are gone,
and the workspace/deny.toml carve-outs that existed only for the vendoring go
with them.

cargo build/test/fmt/clippy all pass for openvtc-vetting-pcs against the
published dependency.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vetting): import build_didcomm_message after the main merge

main moved build_didcomm_message from this file into crate::messaging some
time before this branch's last merge; the merge's textual auto-resolve kept
this file's use block as main had it (which no longer imports the function at
module scope) while leaving hidden_attestation's unqualified call to it
untouched, so it only broke at compile time — cargo build -p
openvtc-vetting-pcs never exercises openvtc-core, so the narrower check run
earlier didn't catch it. Confirmed with a full `cargo build --workspace
--all-targets` and `cargo test --workspace`, both clean.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(ci): force LF for the wire_fixture.rs JSON fixture on Windows

tests/fixtures/submission.json is byte-compared against a freshly
serde_json::to_string_pretty-rendered string (always \n) by
a_submission_round_trips_through_extensions_and_pins_the_fixture. With no
.gitattributes, the Windows CI runner's default core.autocrlf rewrote the
checked-out fixture to \r\n, failing the comparison on content that hadn't
actually changed. The committed blob was already plain LF; this only changes
future checkouts.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

---------

title: feat(vtc-service)!: the policy log and the community's DID log are signed Trust Tasks
body:
## Summary

VTC batch 3, part 1 of a stack: the policy log and the community's own DID log move onto the Trust Task spine, and the per-type size limits come from the specifications.

- **Policies ×6** (`trust_tasks::policy_tasks`): `policy/list/0.2`, `policy/get/0.1`, `policy/active/0.1`, `policy/upsert/0.2`, `policy/activate/0.1`, `vtc/policies/test/0.1`. Authority is the signer's ACL row, read at execution: `Admin`, as the routes' `AdminAuth` asked. `policy/activate` refuses a `purpose` the revision's Rego package does not decide. `policy/list` narrows by `ext["org.openvtc.purpose"]`, the key a revision already names its purpose by (the spec has no purpose filter). Declared codes answered: `policy/get:notFound`, `policy/upsert:versionConflict`, `policy/activate:{notFound,alreadyActive}`, `vtc/policies/test:{notFound,evaluationFailed}`.
- **`did-management/did/register/0.1`**: an unrestricted `Admin` only (the route's `SuperAdminAuth`), authority checked before the payload is read.
- **Size limits** (`trust_tasks/size.rs`): the hand-written table is gone. A type's limit is its specification's `maxDocumentBytes` (`schema_index::max_document_bytes_for`, codegen'd `Payload::MAX_DOCUMENT_BYTES`), otherwise 64 KiB. `policy/upsert/0.2` (192 KiB) and `did/register/0.1` (1 MiB) need more but their specs don't declare it yet, so they sit in `AWAITING_DECLARATION`; a test fails once upstream declares either. #1818's rules still hold: a raised limit applies only to a served type, the HTTPS cap is the largest served limit (now 1 MiB), and no oversized `type` is echoed. New, after webvh #239: a document above 64 KiB gets its type's raised limit only when the claimed `issuer` holds a live ACL entry, or is an active signing-key delegation of one. This is one keyspace read before any verification. Anyone else is held to the default.
- **Console**: every policy call is a signed document (ceremonies, rooms tier probe, repos/bind overview, auto-grant panel).

## Routes

Removed: `GET /v1/policies/active`, `POST /v1/policies/{id}/test`.

title: feat(vtc-service)!: the policy log and the community's DID log are signed Trust Tasks (#1834)
body:
feat(vtc-service)!: the policy log and the community's DID log are signed Trust Tasks (#1834)

policy/{list,get,active,upsert,activate}, vtc/policies/test and
did-management/did/register are served by the spine
(trust_tasks::policy_tasks) on every transport, with the signer's ACL row
as authority: Admin for the policy verbs, an unrestricted Admin for the
DID log, as the bearer routes' AdminAuth and SuperAdminAuth asked.
policy/activate refuses a purpose the revision does not decide. The
console signs every policy call.

Per-type document limits come from the specifications: size.rs reads the
codegen'd maxDocumentBytes (schema_index::max_document_bytes_for) and keeps
an interim entry only for policy/upsert and did/register, whose specs
declare none yet. A raised limit applies to a served type only, and only
when the claimed issuer holds a live ACL entry (or is a signing key
delegated by one), looked up before verification. The HTTPS cap is the
largest served limit; a refusal does not echo an oversized type.

Removed: GET /v1/policies/active, POST /v1/policies/{id}/test.
Kept while vtc-client calls them: GET/POST /v1/policies,
GET /v1/policies/{id}, POST /v1/policies/{id}/activate,
POST /v1/admin/did/register.

title: fix(vtc-service): setup wizard's plaintext choice pins the plaintext backend
body: The wizard's "Plaintext file" choice left `[secrets] backend` unset, so `create_secret_store` fell through its implicit chain to the keyring (when compiled in) and setup failed with "OS credential store is unavailable". The choice now sets `backend = plaintext`. Adds a test pinning it.

title: fix(vtc-service): setup wizard's plaintext choice pins the plaintext backend (#1837)
body:
fix(vtc-service): setup wizard's plaintext choice pins the plaintext backend (#1837)

The interactive wizard's "Plaintext file" choice populated no field, leaving
`SecretsConfig::backend` unset. `create_secret_store` then walked its implicit
chain and picked the OS keyring whenever it is compiled in, so setup failed on
a host without a credential store despite the operator choosing plaintext.
Set the selector explicitly.

This repository is a fork of [etairi/predicate-credential-system](https://github.com/etairi/predicate-credential-system) by [@etairi](https://github.com/etairi) — full credit to them for the original research implementation of the predicate credential system (PCS) this crate is built on. This PR brings that work over and gets the repository ready to stand on its own:

- Preserves the original commit history (`aa57efd` and earlier, authored by @etairi) plus the `application-context` patch that was developed on top of it for OpenVTC's use (previously carried as a vendored patch inside the `openvtc` monorepo).
- Merges in this repository's initial commit so the two histories share a base.
- `Cargo.toml`: adds the `repository` field, drops `publish = false` now that this is its permanent, standalone home.
- Adds CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`): fmt, clippy, tests (all features), a no-default-features build, docs, MSRV (1.95.0) and `cargo package`.
- Adds release-plz-based publishing (`.github/workflows/publish.yml`, `release-plz.toml`, `RELEASING.md`): merging a Release PR tags and publishes to crates.io via Trusted Publishing (OIDC, no long-lived token in the repo).

## Follow-up (manual, outside this PR)

- One-time crates.io Trusted Publishing setup, described in `RELEASING.md`: owner `OpenVTC`, repo `predicate-credential-system`, workflow `publish.yml`, environment `crates-io`.
- Once published, `openvtc` switches its vendored copy over to this crate as a normal dependency.

## Test plan

- [x] `cargo package --locked`
- [x] `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`
- [x] `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
- [ ] CI green on this PR

title: Publish the DTG credential context at /dtg/context/v1 once cred-spec #46 settles
body:
## Summary

Decision 1 in PLAN.md moves the credential `@context` from the First Person placeholder to `https://registry.trustoverip.org/dtg/context/v1`, served frozen from `contexts/v1.jsonld` in this repository. The predicate examples in `predicates/` already list that IRI. Nothing publishes it yet: the spec's Base Structure requires a context that has never been published anywhere, and this repository has no `contexts/` folder.

Writing the context is spec work rather than registry work, which is why it was taken out of the predicates PR. A `v1` context has to define terms for all seven DTG credential types and their members, not only the VSC, and once released it is frozen (GOVERNANCE.md §3, the immutability check). Freezing it before the open naming questions are settled would bake a known gap into a permanent IRI.

## Blocked on

- [trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#48](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/48): the specification's editors recording the credential `@context` IRI as `https://registry.trustoverip.org/dtg/context/v1`, in exactly those bytes (`https`, no `www.`, no trailing slash), and the term namespace `https://registry.trustoverip.org/dtg/credentials#` beside it. Publishing `contexts/v1.jsonld` here has to apply a decision the specification has made, not make one for it. This is the only dependency. The draft is open as #7 so the editors can review the content while deciding the IRI.

## Not blocked on

- [trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#46](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/issues/46). The correlation-scope declaration is one term, and a concrete proposal (`issuerScope`) is in that issue so it can be decided alongside #48. If it is decided before #7 merges, the term goes into `v1`; if not, `v1` is published with what specification 0.5.0 defines and the term goes in `v2`, under the freeze rule in GOVERNANCE.md §3.1. Nothing issued under the First Person IRI is long-lived (see #48), so a `v2` following `v1` costs each implementation one bundle update, and the move away from the First Person IRI already requires that update.
- The seven-type term list being final. `v1` is the context for specification 0.5.0; a later specification version that adds or renames a term mints `v2`. That is the freeze rule working as intended, not a reason to wait.

## What the PR needs to contain

- `contexts/v1.jsonld`: a JSON-LD 1.1 context with `@protected` terms for `DTGCredential`, the seven concrete subtypes, `taskContext`, `taskDigestMultibase`, and the type-specific members of each credential type as specification 0.5.0 defines them. For the VSC: `predicate` as `@id`, `object.id` as a node identifier, `object.value` as `@json`, and `witnessContext`, per the editor's note in the spec's *Statements in the Graph*. `digestMultibase` comes from the W3C VC 2.0 context and is not redefined. The correlation-scope term from #46 is not in `v1`; it arrives in `v2`. Drafted in #7.
- Review by the credential spec editors, since the context is the wire-level shape of every DTG credential, not only the statement ones.
- A check in `scripts/lib/registry.mjs` that every example credential lists the registry's context IRI in `@context`, which can only be turned on once the context exists.
- A matching editorial change in the credential spec: Base Structure's required context IRI, the `dtg:` notation, and the examples.

## Until then

The IRI `https://registry.trustoverip.org/dtg/context/v1` does not resolve; #7 publishes it once merged. Implementations that need a context today carry a bundled copy of the First Person placeholder, as cred-spec #48 records, and the resolution is not load-bearing for any of them.

Refs PLAN.md decision 1 and §1.8 step 3.
author: geoffturk

title: Create the DTG predicate vocabulary as a repo-driven registry
body:
## Summary

#47 introduces the verifiable statement credential (VSC), whose meaning is carried by a predicate from a governed vocabulary, and says that predicates beyond the two core profiles will be defined in a planned "DTG Predicate Vocabulary" specification. Review has already produced the first candidates (#50 identity vetting; presentation/custody in the #47 thread), and the question of where they go is blocking. This issue proposes the answer: **a repo-driven registry, on the model of the ToIP glossary, not a specification** — and lays out what the repository needs to contain so that it can be created and populated without further design work.

The proposal was discussed against the alternative of growing the credential spec, or a dedicated vocabulary spec, and rejected both on cadence: a ToIP specification moves WD → Implementers Draft → Approved Deliverable, and a vocabulary needs to add an entry the week a community needs it. A generated registry governed by pull request is the only shape that matches how the content changes.

Assumption for this issue: ToIP is amenable to hosting the namespace and the published artifacts, at least for now. The IRIs below are placeholders until #48 is decided.

## Three things that were being called "the vocabulary"

| | What it is | Nature | Home |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. The rules** | what a predicate definition must contain, how it is published, immutability, NFC, labels, admission criteria | normative, changes rarely | the credential spec's *Predicate Profiles* section for now (it already states the nine required members); split out into a small "DTG Vocabularies" spec if and when the definition format needs its own normative home |
| **B. WG-curated predicates** | `endorses`, `witnessed`, and whatever the WG agrees to define under the DTG namespace | content, grows one entry at a time | **this repository** |
| **C. Community predicates** | terms a VTC or VTN defines under a namespace it controls | content, not ours to hold | the community's own namespace, referenced from its governance framework; published in the same format as B so tooling works for both |

The credential spec's *Community-Defined Predicates* section keeps one illustrative example and no more; every real predicate goes to B or C.

## The repository

Proposed name: `trustoverip/dtgwg-predicate-vocab`. Same tooling philosophy as `ctwg-main-glossary`: one source file per entry, a generator, a published output, PR governance.

```
dtgwg-predicate-vocab/
├── README.md                     what this is, how to propose a predicate
├── GOVERNANCE.md                 admission criteria, review, statuses, versioning
├── predicates/                   one file per predicate — the source of truth
│   ├── endorses.jsonld
│   ├── witnessed.jsonld
│   ├── identity-vetting.jsonld   from #50
│   └── presented.jsonld          from the #47 review thread
├── schemas/                      JSON Schema for each predicate's `value` payload
│   └── identity-vetting.schema.json
├── meta/
│   ├── predicate.schema.json     the definition format (mirrors the nine points in the credential spec)
│   └── meta-context.jsonld       JSON-LD context for the definition files themselves
├── tools/                        generator: validates predicates/ against meta/, builds dist/
└── dist/                         generated, published at the namespace; never hand-edited
    ├── vocab.jsonld              all active and deprecated terms, additive
    ├── index.html                human-readable vocabulary document
    ├── accept-list.json          machine-readable list verifiers can import
    └── context/
        └── v1.jsonld             frozen context for the additional members of core profiles
```

## The definition format

One JSON-LD document per predicate. The members are the nine points a profile MUST state under *Predicate Profiles* in #47, plus registry metadata. `witnessed`, as it would appear:

```json
{
  "@context": "https://trustoverip.org/dtg/vocab/meta-context.jsonld",
  "id": "https://trustoverip.org/dtg/vocab#witnessed",
  "type": "Predicate",
  "status": "active",
  "since": "2026-10-01",
  "label": {
    "en": "witnessed",
    "de": "bezeugt",
    "nl": "getuige geweest van"
  },
  "definition": {
    "en": "The issuer observed the subject issue the credential the object names, under the conditions of a specific trust task exchange."
  },
  "classification": "evidence",
  "weighedBy": "The community whose witnessing policy the attestation is issued under.",
  "objectKind": ["digestMultibase"],
  "subjectObjectRelationship": "credentialSubject.id MUST be the issuer of the credential object.digestMultibase names; a verifier holding that credential MUST check it.",
  "additionalMembers": {
    "witnessContext": {
      "required": false,
      "schema": "https://trustoverip.org/dtg/vocab/schemas/witness-context.schema.json"
    }
  },
  "taskContextRequired": true,
  "minimumIssuerScope": "directed",
  "issuer": "A member, or a VTA acting according to VTC policy.",
  "establishes": "That the issuer attests that, in the exchange identified by taskContext, it observed the subject issue the credential whose claims digest to object.digestMultibase.",
  "doesNotEstablish": [
    "that the referenced credential is currently valid or unrevoked",
    "that the referenced credential's claims are true",
    "that the exchange reached its terminal state (Outcome Interpretability applies)",
    "that the witness is a member of any community",
    "that any consequential action is authorized"
  ],
  "definedIn": "https://trustoverip.github.io/dtgwg-cred-spec/#the-dtgwitnessed-profile-vwc",
  "governedBy": null
}
```

The presentation/custody predicate from the #47 thread, showing the case where the observed party is the referenced credential's *subject*:

```json
{
  "@context": "https://trustoverip.org/dtg/vocab/meta-context.jsonld",
  "id": "https://trustoverip.org/dtg/vocab#presented",
  "type": "Predicate",
  "status": "proposed",
  "label": { "en": "presented" },
  "definition": {
    "en": "The issuer observed the subject present the credential the object names. The subject is the holder; the credential's issuer need not have been present."
  },
  "classification": "evidence",
  "objectKind": ["digestMultibase"],
  "subjectObjectRelationship": "credentialSubject.id MUST be the credentialSubject.id of the credential object.digestMultibase names.",
  "taskContextRequired": true,
  "minimumIssuerScope": "directed",
  "issuer": "A member, or a VTA acting according to VTC policy.",
  "establishes": "That the issuer attests that, in the exchange identified by taskContext, the subject presented the credential whose claims digest to object.digestMultibase.",
  "doesNotEstablish": [
    "that the presented credential is valid, unrevoked, or was issued to the subject",
    "that the presented credential's claims are true",
    "that the subject controls the presented credential's subject identifier",
    "that any consequential action is authorized"
  ]
}
```

A community predicate uses the same format under its own namespace, with `governedBy` pointing at the governance framework that defines who may issue it and how it is weighed. That is what makes one generator, one validator and one accept-list format serve both tiers.

## Generated outputs

| Artifact | Consumer | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `vocab.jsonld` | tooling, RDF consumers, `rdfs:label` lookups | additive; a term is never removed or altered once active, only deprecated |
| `index.html` | people | the human-readable vocabulary, one section per predicate, labels in every language supplied |
| `accept-list.json` | verifiers | the active IRIs with their machine-checkable constraints (object kinds, `taskContextRequired`, minimum scope, schema URLs), for import into verifier configuration at configuration time |
| `context/v1.jsonld` | credentials under core profiles | the JSON-LD terms for additional members such as `witnessContext`; frozen per version, as VC contexts must be |

An `accept-list.json` entry, so the shape is concrete:

```json
{
  "https://trustoverip.org/dtg/vocab#witnessed": {
    "status": "active",
    "objectKind": ["digestMultibase"],
    "taskContextRequired": true,
    "minimumIssuerScope": "directed",
    "additionalMembers": { "witnessContext": { "required": false } }
  }
}
```

## Versioning and immutability — two different rules

This is the part that needs to be got right before anything is published, and it feeds #48.

- **Predicate IRIs are unversioned and term-immutable.** `…/vocab#witnessed` never changes meaning and is never deleted; adding `#presented` does not touch it. Versioning the namespace (`…/vocab/v1#witnessed` → `…/vocab/v2#witnessed`) would change every predicate's IRI whenever any predicate is added, and break byte-exact matching for every issued credential. So the namespace IRI decided in #48 **must carry no version segment**. The current placeholder in #47 (`https://firstperson.network/credentials/dtg/v1#witnessed`) has one and should not be the final form.
- **Contexts are versioned and frozen.** A JSON-LD context that credentials list must not change after publication, so `context/v1.jsonld` is frozen and additions go in `v2`. This is fine because credentials do not need the vocabulary context to carry a predicate — predicates are absolute IRIs — only to carry a core profile's additional members.

Releases are git tags. `dist/` at a tag is the published state; the namespace serves the latest tag's `vocab.jsonld` and `index.html`, and every `context/vN.jsonld` ever released.

## Governance

`GOVERNANCE.md`, drawing on the credential spec's rules:

- **Not a gate.** The registry curates a shared, trusted default set; it does not decide who may define or use a predicate. Because a predicate is an absolute IRI that a verifier accepts by configuration, resolved at configuration time and never at verification time (Predicate Handling in #47), a community that publishes a predicate under a namespace it controls can issue under it, and verifiers can accept it, without waiting on or ever seeking admission here. #50's identity vetting predicate already works this way. Admission is what a community seeks when it wants convergence — one identifier shared across communities — not what it needs in order to use the standard. The admission criteria below therefore bound what enters the DTG namespace, not what the mechanism permits. This is a stated design guarantee, mirrored in the credential spec's editor's note on where profiles live (#47), not an emergent property.
- **Admission to the DTG namespace.** A proposed predicate is accepted when it (1) is complete against `meta/predicate.schema.json`, including the establishes / does-not-establish block; (2) is on the *attests* side of the statement/establishment test — it is not a predicate whose PASS a verifier would act on as representation, authority, membership, admission, governed status or task completion; (3) is unilateral; (4) is not meaningful only inside one exchange; (5) has no existing term with the same meaning — one identifier per concept; (6) has an NFC IRI and at least an English label; and (7) is either needed by a DTG specification or in use, or credibly about to be, by more than one community.
- **Statuses.** `proposed` (merged, not yet in a release), `active`, `deprecated` (kept forever, marked, with a pointer to any replacement). Nothing is ever deleted.
- **Review.** Two WG approvals for a new `active` term; one for editorial changes to labels or definitions that do not alter meaning; meaning changes are not permitted — deprecate and add.
- **Equivalence.** The registry MAY record that a community term has the same meaning as a DTG term, as information for people configuring verifiers. Verifiers never follow it (Predicate Handling in #47).

## Relationship to the credential spec

- The credential spec keeps the statement mechanism, Predicate Handling, What Verification Establishes, Predicate Profiles (which is where the definition format's requirements live for now), and — for WD03 — the `endorses` and `witnessed` profiles, because they replace WD02 normative text and need a published home. Once this repository has a release, those two move here and the credential spec references them; nothing on the wire changes.
- The `dtg:` notation in the credential spec resolves to this repository's namespace once #48 is decided.
- *Related Specifications* in the credential spec should describe this as a registry, not a specification.
- #50 should target this repository rather than the credential spec's example section, as the first entry.
- #47's reviewer request for a core presentation/custody profile is answered by `presented.jsonld` above rather than by a third profile in the credential spec.

## Sequencing

1. Create the repository with `README.md`, `GOVERNANCE.md`, `meta/`, and an empty `predicates/`; decide #48 so the placeholder IRIs can be replaced.
2. Add the generator (validation against `meta/predicate.schema.json`, build of `dist/`), and CI that fails a PR whose definition is incomplete.
3. First entries: `identity-vetting` (#50), `presented`. Mirror `endorses` and `witnessed` as `proposed` so the format is exercised against the two real profiles.
4. First release once the credential spec reaches WD03; then move `endorses` and `witnessed` here for WD04 and update the credential spec's references.

## Open questions

- Which ToIP deliverable type a repo-driven registry is, and whether the glossary's process and tooling can be borrowed wholesale. (A question for ToIP staff.)
- Whether this repository should also carry the other community-defined vocabularies the DTG already depends on — VDC `scope` terms, VAC `actions`, the VEC endorsement vocabulary — since they are the same kind of thing with the same publication gap. If so, "DTG Vocabularies" is the better name. Flagged, not proposed here.
- Namespace and hosting: #48.

Refs #45, #47, #48, #50, #51.

title: fix(vtc-service): community verbs honour an inviter's scope
body:
Post-merge security review of #1827.

## Fixed

**Invitation verbs were open wider than before.** The bearer routes could only be reached with an admin session, because the VTC mints sessions for admins only. On the signed door, a `Moderator` or `Issuer` can now send `vtc/invitations/*`. Before this fix, such a signer could:
- list every invitation in the community, including each invitee DID, role and issuer;
- revoke any invitation, an administrator's included;
- deliver any invitation;
- mint an invitation that seats the invitee as `moderator`, `issuer` or a custom role.

What changes, below `Admin`:
- **list, revoke and deliver** cover only the invitations the signer issued.
- **Someone else's invitation** is refused exactly as an unknown id is (the same `notFound`), so the answer does not reveal that it exists.
- **issue** may only invite members; conferring a role needs an `Admin`.

`Admin` keeps full access. (`routes/invitations.rs`, `InviterScope`.)

**Weakened test restored.** The graph refusal test in `relationships.rs` had been changed from an `Issuer` session to a plain `Member`. It now checks both.

## Reviewed, no change
- **Members, join-requests, relationships graph, recognition, endorsement-types, solicit-vmc.** The gate is the same as the removed routes: any `Admin` (`AdminAuth`, now `admin_signer`). The VTC treats the community as one scope, as `join-requests/decide` and `members/update` already document. A member's row acts nowhere, so `caller_covers_target` would leave a context admin an empty roster. `MemberResponse` carries no ACL contexts, and pagination and counts match the old routes.
- **Directory.** It projects for the signer, with the role read from the ACL.
- **`tests/common/legacy.rs`.** Every original assertion is still sent to the real operation. Two limits remain:
  - An unmapped token gets a 401 that the adapter makes up itself. The signed-door `proofRequired` and `permissionDenied` tests in `community_verbs_spine.rs` cover the real refusals.
  - The status is derived from the refusal code. That is loose, but no test relies on an ambiguous mapping.
- **Removed routes.** Nothing in the console, `vtc-client`, `cnm-cli` or the tests still calls them. `vtc-client` still uses `GET /v1/members` and `GET /v1/join-requests`, which are kept. A stale comment in `profile.tsx` is updated.

## Checks
- `cargo clippy -p vtc-service --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt` are clean.
- Tests run: `community_verbs_spine` (11 passed, including the new `an_inviter_below_admin_manages_only_its_own_invitations`), `relationships` (60 passed), `invitations` (13 passed).

title: fix(vtc-service): charge signed Trust Tasks to the signer, not the anonymous governor
body:
`POST /v1/trust-tasks` sat behind the per-address unauthenticated governor (a burst of 10, then one per 5 s). With the console's reads now signed Trust Tasks (#1824, #1827), operators hit it while navigating.

This was meant to land on #1827, which merged first. It carries the rate-limit half of #1824's leftover work. The authorisation half is already on main via #1829.

**Budgets** (`vtc-service/src/routing/trust_task_admission.rs`):

| document | charged |
|---|---|
| unsigned, or claiming a DID with no live ACL entry | the strict per-address bucket (the tower governor's own limiter state, so there is no second anonymous budget), before verification |
| claiming a known DID (a live ACL row, or a console key whose delegating admin has one) | a per-address ceiling (120, then one per 250 ms) before verification; then the signer's bucket (60, then one per 500 ms), keyed by the principal, once the proof verifies |
| a known-DID claim that fails verification | the strict per-address bucket as well |

Fresh DIDs never get a bucket. The spine consults the transport after the proof verifies and before the duplicate-execution record is claimed (`dispatch_trust_task_core_admitted`), so a refused document keeps its `id` for the retry.

**Tests**
- Admission unit tests.
- `rate_limit_source`: an ACL signer sends 30 requests from one address and none is refused; an unknown signer is refused on the 11th.
- `test_support_smoke::minted_admin_token_is_accepted` and the CORS preflight tests in `routing_cors` targeted the removed `GET /v1/admin/config`. They now point at `/v1/audit/verify` (which also asserts the anonymous 401) and `/v1/trust-tasks`.

Local checks: clippy `-D warnings`, fmt, and the four suites above. CI runs the rest.

title: fix(vtc-service): charge signed Trust Tasks to the signer, not the anonymous governor (#1832)
body:
fix(vtc-service): charge signed Trust Tasks to the signer, not the anonymous governor (#1832)

* fix(vtc-service): charge signed Trust Tasks to the signer, not the anonymous governor

`POST /v1/trust-tasks` sat behind the per-address unauthenticated governor
(a burst of 10, then one per 5 s). With the console's reads now signed Trust
Tasks, an administrator hit it while navigating.

The door now charges each document to a budget chosen by who signed it
(`routing::trust_task_admission`):

- unsigned documents, and ones claiming a DID with no live ACL entry, pay
  the strict per-address bucket before verification. It is the tower
  governor's own limiter state, so an address gets no second anonymous
  budget;
- documents claiming a known DID (a live ACL row, or a console key whose
  delegating admin has one) first pay a per-address ceiling (120, then one
  per 250 ms) that bounds verification work;
- once verified, they pay the signer's bucket (60, then one per 500 ms),
  keyed by the principal, so console keys share their admin's bucket;
- a known-DID claim that fails verification pays the strict bucket too.

Fresh DIDs never get a bucket. The spine asks the transport once the proof
has verified and before the duplicate-execution record is claimed
(`dispatch_trust_task_core_admitted`), so a refused document keeps its id.

Also points `minted_admin_token_is_accepted` and the CORS preflight tests,

title: feat(vtc-service)!: the administrator's community verbs are signed Trust Tasks
body:
Stacked on #1824. Second batch of admin-facing b1 verbs (inventory 2026-09-28) onto the Trust Task spine.

## What moves

`trust_tasks::community_tasks` serves these over TSP, DIDComm and HTTPS. Authority is the verified signer's ACL row, read when the document runs:

| task | authority |
|---|---|
| `vtc/community/profile/show/0.1`, `vtc/ceremonies/list/0.1` | any entry (the route took any session) |
| `vtc/directory/query/0.1` | any entry, as the viewer the directory policy projects for |
| `vtc/endorsement-types/list/0.1`, `vtc/recognition/check/0.1` | Admin |
| `vtc/members/{list,removed,show,solicit-vmc}/0.1` | Admin |
| `vtc/join-requests/{list,show}/0.1` | Admin |
| `vtc/relationships/graph/0.2` | Admin |
| `vtc/invitations/{issue,list,revoke,deliver}/0.1` | Admin, Moderator or Issuer (the operation's own check) |

A VTC bearer session could only be minted for an administrator. So the reads any entry may make, and the inviter verbs, now reach the members their handlers already admitted.

- `invitations/issue` (the VIC) and `invitations/deliver` (the offer code) carry bearer secrets. The duplicate-execution record keeps no copy of them, so a redelivered document gets `204`.
- `invitations/deliver` refusals carry the declared codes (`notFound`, `revoked`, `noRoute`), and a lapsed invitation is `expired`.
- The console signs every one of these: members, join requests, profile, ceremonies, recognition, graph, invitations, the name book, and the pickers in Repos and Vetting.

## Routes

Removed: `GET /v1/community/profile`, `GET /v1/ceremonies`, `GET /v1/directory/{did}`, `GET /v1/endorsement-types`, `GET /v1/recognition/check`, `GET /v1/members/removed`, `GET /v1/members/{did}`, `POST /v1/members/{did}/request-vmc`, `GET /v1/join-requests/{id}`, `GET /v1/relationships/graph`, `GET`+`POST /v1/invitations`, `DELETE /v1/invitations/{id}`, `POST /v1/invitations/deliver`.

Kept because vtc-client still calls them: `GET /v1/members` (`list_members`) and `GET /v1/join-requests` (`list_join_requests`). Both are also served on the spine.

## Not in this stack yet

The third batch is still to do: `policy/{list,upsert,active,get,activate}` and `vtc/policies/test`, `did-management/did/register`, and `vtc/website/{files/list,files/delete,generations/list,rollback}`. For those, vtc-client's `list_policies`, `get_policy`, `upload_policy`, `activate_policy` and `install_did_log` would keep their routes. `policy/upsert` and `did/register` get their raised size limits once they are dispatched.

## Tests

`tests/community_verbs_spine.rs`: for every moved verb, an authorized signer is answered (signed reply, `#response` schema), unsigned is `proofRequired`, a signer the community doesn't know is `permissionDenied`, a member is refused the admin and inviter verbs, a moderator is refused the admin verbs, the routes are gone, the vtc-client listings keep theirs, and a redelivered issue doesn't hand the credential out again. `solicit-vmc` has its own test: the fixture member has no transport to push to, so the test holds that authority passes and the push is attempted.

The existing suites (`ceremonies_list`, `community_profile`, `directory`, `invitations`, `members_crud`, `join_requests`, `relationships`, `join_didcomm`, `endorsements`, `install_flow`) now go through the signed door. `tests/common/legacy.rs` turns the requests these suites used to send to a retired route into the signed document for that route, so their assertions are unchanged.

## Checks

Local results are in the comments below.

title: fix(vtc-service): printed pnm acl create grant carries --handoff
body:
The VTC setup wizard's "context already exists" fallback printed `pnm acl create --did … --role admin --contexts … --expires 1h` without `--handoff`. Provisioning rolls the setup DID over to a VTA-minted long-term admin, which the VTA refuses without a one-time hand-off (VTI-ACL-053, VTI-ACL-054), so following the printed command fails with `forbidden … carries no one-time hand-off`.

Fixed in:
- `vtc-service/src/setup/wizard.rs`: the wizard's fallback grant
- `vtc-service/src/emergency.rs`: the emergency-bootstrap hint (AdminRotated also rolls over)
- `docs/03-vtc/getting-started.md`, `docs/03-vtc/examples/vtc-setup.example.toml`

All of these now match `vta_sdk::provision_client::authz::grant_hint`.

Checks run: `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo check -p vtc-service`. The full test suite was not run.

title: feat(vta): vta contexts update --clear-did, offline
body:
Follow-up to #1828. `pnm contexts update` gained `--clear-did` there, but the offline `vta` binary's `contexts update` could still only set a DID. #1828 listed this as not done.

- `vta contexts update <id> --clear-did` conflicts with `--did`, as in pnm.
- The clear goes through `operations::contexts::update_context_did(None)`, the same operation `vta/contexts/update-did/1.1` uses. `update_context` only ever sets a DID. A name or description change in the same command still goes through `update_context` first.
- The DID itself is not deleted, so it can then be deleted or assigned again.

**Checks:** `cargo fmt` and `cargo check -p vta-service --bins` are clean. At the author's request, to get this out quickly, **no tests were run locally**; this relies on CI. No new tests: it's a CLI flag over an operation #1828 already covers.

title: feat(console): clear a context's DID, over vta/contexts/update-did/1.1
body:
## Why

In the console's Identity panel you could pick **— none —** for a context's DID, but the agent had no way to do it. Choosing it sent `did: ""` on `vta/contexts/update-did/1.0`, whose schema requires a non-empty string, and the request was refused with `"" is shorter than 1 character`. It hurt most right after a DID deletion failed with "context `vtc` acts as this DID — reassign it first", because there was no way to retire a context's last DID.

trust-tasks#684 added `update-did/1.1`, where `did` may be `null` to clear it and a string must be a real DID. It's released in `@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.21.13. OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1828 serves 1.1 on the VTA.

## What

- **core:** `contextsUpdateDid` sends 1.1 and takes `did: string | null`.
- **console:** "none" sends `null`, never `""`. The button reads **Clear DID**, and the panel says the DID itself isn't deleted: it stays under DIDs and can be assigned again or deleted.
- **`@openvtc/trust-tasks` floor `^0.21.13`**, the first release carrying 1.1. This is a correctness floor, because below it the import doesn't resolve.
- **`task-surface.json`** re-synced from vta-sdk, with update-did/1.1 included.

Two fixes surfaced along the way, each in its own commit:

- **`sync-task-surface.mjs` resolves a fully qualified generated type.** Since VTI #1790, vta-sdk writes a dozen constants as `<trust_tasks_rs::specs::…::Payload as trust_tasks_rs::Payload>::TYPE_URI`. The resolver only followed `pub use` aliases, so every sync stopped on them and the snapshot hadn't been refreshable since.
- **`auth/revoke-session/0.2`.** #1790 moved that task to 0.2 and stopped serving 0.1, so the console's session revoke has been refused since. For the member it sends (`sessionId`), 0.2 is a superset of 0.1. The first sync the previous fix made possible surfaced this.

**This cuts over with #1828**, per the no-compatibility-folds rule: a VTA without 1.1 refuses it as an unsupported task. Merge #1828 first. The snapshot was synced from #1828's branch, and I'll re-sync from main once it lands if anything moved.

## Tests

title: feat(vta): clear a context's DID with vta/contexts/update-did/1.1
body:
Serves `vta/contexts/update-did/1.1` (trust-tasks #684, released in `trust-tasks-rs` 0.24.6), where `did: null` clears a context's DID. 1.0 is still served.

**Why.** Once a context had a DID, it could only be replaced. 1.0 requires a non-empty `did`, and `vta/contexts/update` only ever sets one. The DID-delete blocker told the operator to reassign the DID first, so the only way to retire a context's last DID was to assign one they didn't want. The browser console already offered "none" and was refused with `"" is shorter than 1 character`.

**Behaviour:**
- 1.0 and 1.1 share one handler. 1.1 parses into the generated `update_did::v1_1::Payload`, and 1.0 still parses into `UpdateContextDidBody`.
- `update_context_did` takes `Option<String>`. `None` removes the DID, and the returned record omits `did`. Clearing an already-clear context succeeds, and only `updatedAt` changes. The log line says "cleared" or "updated".
- A 1.1 request with a missing `did`, `""`, `did:` or a non-DID string is refused `malformedRequest` by the dispatch spine's schema check, before serde could read a missing member as a clear.
- Deprecation table: 1.0 is superseded by 1.1, and legacy `PUT /contexts/{id}/did` names 1.1 as its successor. It still only sets a DID.
- 1.1 is added to the dispatch table, the conformance sweep, the `notFound` sweep, and `retry_safety` (RetrySafe).

**CLI** (pnm and cnm):
- `pnm contexts update-did <id> --clear`: the DID argument becomes optional and conflicts with `--clear`.
- `pnm contexts update <id> --clear-did`: conflicts with `--did`. The clear goes through update-did, and a name or description change still goes through `contexts/update`.

**DID-delete blocker** now offers both, and names update-did, which a context admin can run. The old `contexts update --did` needed super-admin.
```
context `{id}` acts as this DID — reassign it first: `pnm contexts update-did {id} <new-did>`, or leave the context with no DID: `pnm contexts update-did {id} --clear`
```

**SDK:** the public API is non-breaking. `update_context_did(id, did)` keeps its signature and now sends 1.1. `VtaClient::clear_context_did(id)` is new.

**Floor:** `trust-tasks-rs` and `trust-tasks-capability-client` go to 0.24.6. That is a correctness floor: below it `TASK_CONTEXTS_UPDATE_DID_1_1` doesn't compile, and the spine has no schema for `did: null`.

**Cuts over with** the browser console (`pnm-browser-plugin`), which sends `did: null` on 1.1. That PR follows this one.

**Checks run locally:**
- Before the rebase:
  - `cargo test -p vta-sdk -p vta-service -p vta-cli-common -p pnm-cli` against the released 0.24.6: 3168 passed, 0 failed.
  - `cargo test --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client` with a local trust-tasks patch: 5156 passed.
  - `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check`: clean.
- After rebasing onto current main: `cargo check --all-targets` on the changed crates only.
- Not run locally: `vtc-service`/`vtc-client` and the reduced-feature clippy runs.

New tests:
- `clearing_a_context_did_removes_it_and_is_idempotent`
- `contexts_update_did_1_1_clears`, which also sends 1.0
- `contexts_update_did_1_1_refuses_a_non_did`
- 1.1 rows in the `notFound` and conformance sweeps

**Not done:** the offline `vta` binary's `contexts update --did` (`vta-service/src/main.rs`) has no clear option yet.

title: fix(vtc-service): config writes and admin invites need an unrestricted admin
body:
A security fix for a gap #1824 carried over from the REST handlers when it moved them to the spine.

**High.** `vtc/config/{patch,reload,restart}` and `vtc/config/import` asked only for an admin, as the old REST `AdminAuth` did. So an admin scoped to a single context could:
- lower `acl.unrestricted_admin_consent_threshold`, the APV-014 consent requirement;
- change `public_url` or `server.*`;
- restart the process repeatedly.

All four now require an **unrestricted** admin.

**Medium.** `vtc/admin/invites/{list,revoke}` were open to context admins, although an invite confers unrestricted authority. They now require an unrestricted admin. `create` refuses a context admin up front, including on the TTL-too-long path.

**Tests:**
- the context-admin refusal list in `tests/admin_verbs_spine.rs` now includes the config writes and invites;
- `tests/admin_config.rs::import_refuses_a_context_admin` covers import.

Checks: `admin_config` (36) and `admin_verbs_spine` (17) pass, and `cargo clippy -p vtc-service --all-targets -D warnings` and fmt are clean.

**Follow-ups, not in this PR:**
- An unrestricted admin can lower the consent threshold alone; lowering it should itself need consent at the current threshold.
- There is no restart cooldown.
- The per-signer rate-limit bucket for `/v1/trust-tasks` goes with #1827.
- Two tests pass without testing anything, because they point at the removed `GET /v1/admin/config`: `test_support_smoke::minted_admin_token_is_accepted` and the CORS preflight tests in `routing_cors.rs`.
